text: For giving color to the grain of leather, the book rates vinegar black above every other blacking.

The simplest and best vinegar black: cover shavings from an iron turner with pure cider vinegar, heat up and set aside for a week or two, heat again and set in a cool place for two weeks, pour off the vinegar, let it stand a few days, then draw off and cork in bottles.
Vinegar black made from iron shavings and cider vinegar keeps for a long time and gives a deep black on leather without staining the hands.
A second vinegar black is made by covering iron scraps with sour beer, letting them stand for a month or more, then straining off the beer and bottling it.
A third vinegar black: boil sulphate of iron in vinegar; mix brewers' yeast with beer and let it stand twenty-four hours, then skim off the yeast and add the vinegar.
Logwood black: boil 1 pound of ground logwood, half a pound of nut galls and 1 ounce of verdigris in 1 gallon of water for two hours, let it stand until cold, and strain off the liquor.

A wax for finishing edges: to 1 pint of logwood black add a quarter pound of white wax, half a pound of brown sugar and half a pound of bone black rubbed smooth in turpentine, and heat until thoroughly amalgamated.

Another logwood black: boil logwood bark in double its bulk of rain water for two or three hours, strain, and add a quarter pound of potash to 2 gallons of the liquor; it is a good grain black as well as edge black.
Hatters' black, described as unequaled for finishing: dissolve 1 pound of extract of logwood, half an ounce of bichromate of potash and 1 ounce of copperas in 1 gallon of water.
A second hatters' black formula: dissolve 1 pound of extract of logwood, 2 ounces of copperas and one and a half ounces of bichromate of potash in one and a half gallons of water.

Ball black: melt together 8 ounces of beef suet, 2 ounces of neat's-foot oil, 2 ounces of white wax and 2 ounces of pulverized gum arabic; add 1 gill of turpentine and enough bone black for a good color; stir until cold and roll into balls.
Ball black is applied by warming the ball, rubbing it on the leather, and polishing with a woolen cloth.
English ball blacking for harness is composed of 1 ounce of lard, 1 ounce of beeswax, 8 ounces of ivory black, 8 ounces of sugar, 4 ounces of linseed oil and 2 or 3 ounces of water.

One ball blacking is made of 2 ounces of hog's lard, 8 ounces of neat's-foot oil, 2 ounces of beeswax, 10 ounces of ivory black and 8 ounces of water, heated to a boil, stirred until cool, and formed into balls about two inches in diameter.

Liquid black: mix bone black with equal parts of neat's-foot oil and brown sugar into a thick paste, and thin it with vinegar and sulphuric acid in the proportion of three parts vinegar to one of acid.

Liebig's black: mix bone black with half its weight of molasses and one eighth its weight of olive oil, then add half its weight of hydrochloric acid and one fourth its weight of strong sulphuric acid, with water enough for a thin paste.

Patent harness black: heat 2 ounces of white wax and 3 ounces of turpentine over a slow fire; when the wax is dissolved add 1 ounce of ivory black and 1 dram of indigo, and stir until cold. Apply with a cloth and polish with a shoe brush.

Waterproof paste blacking: melt 4 ounces of black resin and 6 ounces of beeswax over a slow fire, add 1 ounce of lampblack and a quarter pound of finely powdered Prussian blue, and add turpentine enough for a thin paste.
Crown soap black: dissolve over a slow fire 1 pound of beeswax, 1 pound of crown soap, 3 ounces of indigo, 4 ounces of ivory black and half a pint of oil of turpentine, then stir until cold.

Finishing black: mix half an ounce each of gelatin and indigo, 8 ounces of extract of logwood, 2 ounces of crown soap, 8 ounces of softened glue and 1 quart of vinegar over a slow fire. Apply with a soft brush and polish with a woolen cloth.
Cordova wax: mix one and a half pints of red (chromic) acid, 1 pint of beer, 1 gill of thick glue, 2 ounces of ivory black and 1 dram of indigo; boil for half an hour and apply with a sponge.

German blacking: melt 2 pounds of softened glue, add 2 pounds of castile soap dissolved in warm water, then half a pound of yellow wax in small pieces, then half a pint of neat's-foot oil and enough lampblack for the color wanted.

Anilin black: mix 1 dram of fine anilin black with 60 drops of concentrated hydrochloric acid and one and a half ounces of alcohol, giving a deep blue liquid; diluted with one and a half ounces of shellac dissolved in alcohol it gives a beautiful black.

Blacking for restoring harness: mix 1 ounce of indigo, 1 pound of extract of logwood, 1 ounce of softened glue and 8 ounces of crown soap in 2 quarts of vinegar over a slow fire. Apply with a soft brush and polish with a harder one.

Blacking for patent or enameled leather: half a pound each of ivory black, purified lampblack and pulverized indigo, 3 ounces of dissolved gum arabic, 4 ounces of brown sugar and a quarter ounce of glue dissolved in 1 pint of water, boiled, stirred cool and rolled into balls.

Blacking for restoring leather covered mountings: melt 3 parts of white wax, add 1 part gum copal dissolved in linseed oil and 1 part ivory black, boil five minutes, stir until cool and roll into balls.
Blacking for the flesh side: mix 1 pound of prime lampblack with 12 pounds of pure neat's-foot oil, then add 6 pounds of good tallow, melted, while hot; mix well and use when cold.
Rein leather is usually stained by the currier, but the freshly cut edges need to be stained in the workshop to match the grain.
Workshop stains for russet leather are generally made of Spanish saffron and anotta, or of saffron alone.
The most common russet stain: boil saffron in water until the color is extracted, cut anotta in urine, and mix the two; the more anotta used, the darker the color.
Another russet stain: boil half an ounce of Spanish saffron and a quarter ounce of anotta in water until the dye is extracted, then add some alcohol to set the color.
In a stain made of saffron alone, alcohol is added when cold to set the color, and the shade can be changed by adding oxalic acid in varying quantities.
Saffron and anotta stains are applied with a cloth and, when nearly dry, rubbed with a woolen rag slightly waxed.
A yellow stain is produced by boiling fustic berries in alum water; the shade is darkened by adding a small quantity of powdered Brazilwood boiled with the berries.
A brown stain is made by boiling equal parts of pine and alder barks in six times their bulk of water until the color is extracted, and adding a small quantity of alcohol when cold.
Saffron boiled for twelve or fifteen hours gives a good brown stain, to which alcohol must be added to make it set.
Picric acid and water in proportions of 1 to 10, heated to blood heat, make a good yellow stain; wold boiled in water also makes a yellow stain.
The orange yellow stain from fustic berries boiled in alum water turns into a rich brown if the leather is washed with an alkali before the stain is fairly dry.
A red stain is produced by boiling Brazilwood in lye; mixed with wold it gives a brownish yellow well adapted for halters and bridles.
An edge stain for russet leather: cut 4 ounces of anotta in 2 quarts of urine, let it stand twenty-four hours, add 3 quarts of water and boil until reduced to one half the original quantity.
All stains look better and last longer when covered with a little shellac varnish, applied with a sponge after the reins are all dry.

Shellac varnish: dissolve 6 parts of shellac in as little alcohol as possible, mix with 3 parts of Venetian turpentine and heat; when cool add half a part of fine bone black and half a part of oil of lavender, all by weight, then thin with turpentine.
Elastic varnish: dissolve half a pound of gum caoutchouc in ether, add half a pound each of linseed oil and spirits of turpentine, boil over a slow fire until clear, and strain.
To make elastic varnish harder and quicker drying, use half the quantity of gum caoutchouc and substitute the best gum copal for the remainder.

German leather varnish: dissolve pulverized copal gum moistened with turpentine over a moderate fire for about ten hours, pour it into double its quantity of nearly boiling linseed oil, heat, thin with spirits of turpentine, strain, bottle and set in the sun to ripen.
German leather varnish is an excellent varnish for horse collars; on collars that have lost their color a little bone black should be added.

Waterproof varnish: dissolve 1 pound of pulverized shellac in alcohol in a tightly corked bottle kept warm; to a quart of the liquid add 1 ounce of ivory black and half an ounce of gum camphor dissolved in alcohol.
Black varnish for japanned work: dissolve 2 pounds of asphaltum in 1 pint of boiled linseed oil in an iron pot until fused, cool a little, add 2 quarts of spirits of turpentine and stir until cold.
Black varnish for japanned work is used for retouching japanned mountings and seats where the japan has scaled off.

French polish: beat 5 pounds of stearin into thin sheets, mix with 7 pounds of oil of turpentine, heat in a water bath, and when hot add half an ounce of ivory or bone black, stirring to prevent crystallization.

Polish for patent leather: mix the whites of two eggs, 1 teaspoonful of spirits of wine, 1 ounce of sugar and enough finely pulverized ivory black for the shade wanted. Apply with a sponge and polish with a piece of silk.

Wax polish: melt together 1 pound of white wax, 1 pound of crown soap, 5 ounces of ivory black, 1 ounce of indigo and half a pint of nut oil over a slow fire, stir until cool and turn into small moulds.

German leather polish: soften 1 part of white glue in water, add 3 parts of crown soap and heat; mix in 3 parts of bone black moistened with vinegar and 1 part of wheat starch beaten smooth in cold water, and keep over a slow fire for half an hour.
German leather polish is used by dissolving a small quantity in sour beer or vinegar and applying it with a brush as thinly as possible.
